source.title: Effective deep learning for oral exfoliative cytology classification
source.authors: S. Sukegawa; Futa Tanaka; K. Nakano; T. Hara; Kazumasa Yoshii; Katsusuke Yamashita; S. Ono; Kiyofumi Takabatake; Hotaka Kawai; H. Nagatsuka; Y. Furuki

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether optimizer and learning-rate scheduling change the training–validation gap using VGG16 on natural cytology images; this is a conceptual test of optimizer effects on generalization.
record.gate_note: Reports learning curves and classification metrics for SGD and SAM, with and without a learning-rate scheduler. The grid-search results for selecting ρ are not catalog rows; cited results from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study compares SGD with SGD-based SAM and learning-rate scheduling on cytology images. None of its results tests V1–V8: SAM is not an adaptive optimizer comparison under V4, and optimizing unscaled neighborhood sharpness does not measure the magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization correlation or measure rankings in V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: scheduled SAM achieved their preferred classification performance within 300 epochs and tended to suppress overfitting. Their highest-performance wording needs qualification: SAM led accuracy and AUC, while scheduled SGD led recall and F1.
record.recipe_differences: A VGG16 medical-image classification study comparing SAM and momentum SGD, with and without warm-up and step-decay scheduling. It did not test the claim’s random-label memorization/generalization recipe or the versions’ specified conditions.
record.method_sensitivity: The scheduler changed classification metrics; scheduler-related improvement was reported for all SAM metrics except precision, and for all SGD metrics except precision. The qualitative training–validation gap comparison was between SAM and SGD.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM showed a qualitatively smaller training–validation dissociation and less tendency to overfit than SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SGD-based SAM can reduce overfitting relative to momentum SGD for fine-tuned VGG16 on oral cytology tiles.

fits_no_version.finding: Scheduling improved accuracy, recall, F1 and AUC for both optimizers; SGD precision decreased and SAM precision did not change significantly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Warm-up and step-decay scheduling improve several held-out classification metrics in this cytology training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: With scheduling, SAM exceeded SGD in accuracy, precision and AUC but had lower recall and F1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM's advantage over SGD on oral cytology classification depends on the performance metric.

record.problems: Single-facility data with no external validation; positive and negative label counts were imbalanced (881 versus 5113); results are from one architecture and one batch size; no random-label or memorization-capacity test; training–validation gap comparison is qualitative and lacks reported numerical gap values.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results meeting the row rule were omitted.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and local-connectivity effects.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects and remedies under fixed epoch budgets; batch size is always 32.
Dropout effects and interactions with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with generalization gaps, and its ranking against other measures.
Removing highly memorized versus randomly selected examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: No verdicts apply to V1–V8. References to optimizer comparisons and warm-up do not constitute tests of V4 or V5. The supplied text contains Figure 2's caption and qualitative interpretation, but no readable numerical learning-curve gaps.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence were not tested.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
No adaptive optimizer such as Adam was tested against SGD; SAM is the optimizer intervention studied.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measure or comparison of sharpness measures.
No memorized-example removal or retraining comparison.

rows.subject: VGG16 CNN model, SGD
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD with momentum, without learning-rate scheduler; assessed over 30 repetitions.
rows.measure: Accuracy; precision; recall; F1 score; AUC
rows.value: Accuracy 0.8879; precision 0.8518; recall 0.6501; F1 score 0.6937; AUC 0.9020
rows.uncertainty: SD: 0.0016, 0.0099, 0.0089, 0.0095, 0.0075 respectively; 95% CIs are reported in Table 1.
rows.note: Held-out classification metrics, but the study does not report a training–test error gap for this condition.
rows.check: Table 1 values are correctly transcribed but do not measure any claim version. Describe the model as ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 fine-tuned on cytology images; ImageNet was not the fine-tuning dataset.

rows.subject: VGG16 CNN model, SGD
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SGD with momentum and warm-up plus step-decay learning-rate scheduler; assessed over 30 repetitions.
rows.measure: Accuracy; precision; recall; F1 score; AUC
rows.baseline: SGD without scheduler: accuracy 0.8879; precision 0.8518; recall 0.6501; F1 score 0.6937; AUC 0.9020
rows.value: Accuracy 0.8970; precision 0.8049; recall 0.7581; F1 score 0.7780; AUC 0.9098
rows.uncertainty: SD: 0.0026, 0.0066, 0.0064, 0.0057, 0.0030 respectively; 95% CIs reported in Table 1. Scheduler comparisons: p < .0001 for all metrics; effect sizes 4.143, 5.463, 13.721, 10.609, 1.348 respectively.
rows.note: Scheduler improved all reported SGD metrics except precision, per text. These are held-out metrics, not a direct measure of the training–test gap.
rows.check: Values match Tables 1–2 but test scheduling rather than any claim version. Correct the training-stage description to ImageNet pretraining followed by cytology fine-tuning.

rows.subject: VGG16 CNN model, SAM
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SAM, without learning-rate scheduler; assessed over 30 repetitions.
rows.measure: Accuracy; precision; recall; F1 score; AUC
rows.value: Accuracy 0.8870; precision 0.8529; recall 0.6438; F1 score 0.6872; AUC 0.8766
rows.uncertainty: SD: 0.0004, 0.0024, 0.0017, 0.0019, 0.0069 respectively; 95% CIs reported in Table 1.
rows.note: Held-out classification metrics, but no training–test error gap is reported for this condition.
rows.check: Values match Table 1 but test no claim version. SAM uses SGD as its base optimizer. Correct the training-stage description to ImageNet pretraining followed by cytology fine-tuning.

rows.subject: VGG16 CNN model, SAM
rows.operation_detail: Trained with SAM and warm-up plus step-decay learning-rate scheduler; assessed over 30 repetitions.
rows.measure: Accuracy; precision; recall; F1 score; AUC
rows.baseline: SAM without scheduler: accuracy 0.8870; precision 0.8529; recall 0.6438; F1 score 0.6872; AUC 0.8766
rows.value: Accuracy 0.9016; precision 0.8534; recall 0.7139; F1 score 0.7578; AUC 0.9328
rows.uncertainty: SD: 0.0018, 0.0072, 0.0124, 0.0098, 0.0016 respectively; 95% CIs reported in Table 1. Scheduler comparisons: accuracy p < .0001, effect size 11.226; precision p = 0.733, effect size 0.090; recall p < .0001, effect size 7.832; F1 p < .0001, effect size 9.894; AUC p < .0001, effect size 10.997.
rows.note: Authors report improved SAM performance with scheduler except precision, and describe SAM with scheduler as highest performing. Held-out metrics do not directly measure the training–test gap.
rows.check: Values match Tables 1–2 but test no claim version. SAM with scheduling has the highest accuracy and AUC, while scheduled SGD has higher recall and F1. Correct the training-stage description to ImageNet pretraining followed by cytology fine-tuning.

rows.subject: VGG16 CNN model, SGD
rows.operation_detail: Compared training and validation learning curves across increasing epochs.
rows.measure: Dissociation between training and validation accuracy and loss; overfitting
rows.baseline: VGG16 CNN model, SAM, corresponding scheduler condition
rows.value: Authors state SGD showed overfitting with increasing epochs and a larger training–validation dissociation than SAM.
rows.locator: Results, “Comparison of learning curves between optimizer SAM and SGD with and without a learning rate scheduler”; Figure 2
rows.note: Qualitative description; no numerical gap values are provided.
rows.check: Change reversed to cannot_determine: greater overfitting with SGD than SAM is not a reversal of any supplied version. The qualitative learning-curve description is supported by the Results.

rows.subject: VGG16 CNN model, SAM
rows.operation_detail: Compared training and validation learning curves across increasing epochs.
rows.measure: Dissociation between training and validation accuracy and loss; overfitting
rows.baseline: VGG16 CNN model, SGD, corresponding scheduler condition
rows.value: Authors state the training–validation dissociation was smaller in SAM than SGD and SAM tended to be less likely to show overfitting as epochs increased.
rows.locator: Results, “Comparison of learning curves between optimizer SAM and SGD with and without a learning rate scheduler”; Figure 2
rows.note: Qualitative description; no numerical gap values are provided. The authors say SAM tended to suppress overfitting, rather than that it eliminated it.
rows.check: The qualitative smaller training–validation gap is supported, but no magnitude-aware sharpness measurement, matched-low-loss comparison, or correlation ranking is reported.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
